gaps.sentence: ___ time I visit Rome, I discover something new.
gaps.explanation: 'Every time I ...' introduces repeated occasions; 'all time' and 'whole time' are not used here.

gaps.sentence: He isn't old ___ to drive a car.
gaps.explanation: 'Old enough' means sufficiently old; 'enough' follows the adjective, while 'too' gives the opposite meaning.

gaps.sentence: Three out of four respondents — that is, the ___ — supported the change.
gaps.hint: three out of four = more than half
gaps.explanation: Three out of four is more than half, so 'the majority' is the correct label.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the two proposals has been approved so far.
gaps.explanation: 'Neither of the two' — 'none' is for three or more.

gaps.hint: price per item comes at the end
gaps.explanation: 'Fifteen pounds each' means fifteen pounds per ticket; 'every' cannot stand alone in this position.

gaps.sentence: There was ___ enthusiasm for the proposal, so it was quietly shelved.
gaps.explanation: 'Little' (without 'a') means not enough — which explains shelving the proposal.

gaps.sentence: Have we got ___ eggs for breakfast?
gaps.explanation: 'Any' is the normal quantifier in neutral questions; 'none' cannot stand before a noun.

gaps.sentence: I put ___ sugar in your tea by mistake.
gaps.explanation: 'Too much' is used before uncountable nouns like sugar; 'too sugar' is impossible.
